summary:
Cuba's constitutional and statutory framework protects gender identity in its terms. Article 42 of the 2019 Constitution names sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories, the first constitution anywhere to do so.

The 2022 Family Code, approved by referendum on 25 September 2022 with 66.87% support, legalised same-sex marriage and adoption and provides for legal gender change without surgery. Consensual same-sex relations were removed from the Penal Code in 1979.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than surgical or judicial. The July 2025 civil-registry reform removed the remaining bureaucratic hurdles to name changes, and the Family Code already established that surgery is not a precondition.

Trans healthcare sits inside the public system: Resolution 126 of 2008 brought trans medical care into state health provision.

Employment protection is narrower than the constitutional text. The Labor Code (Law 116) bars discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation, but its article 2(b) covers orientation rather than gender identity as a separate protected ground.

The 2013 parliamentary amendment that prohibited employment discrimination on sexual orientation was approved after intense debate. Mariela Castro of CENESEX proposed extending the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status; that trans-specific extension drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, but the confirmed outcome was the sexual-orientation ban.
tangentialFactors:
The equality settlement is contested rather than uniformly state-enforced. Opponents of the 2022 Family Code cited religious objections and feared that its child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No solely to deny the incumbent administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown, which produced more than 1,400 arrestees, and record emigration.

The historical arc shapes what a visitor sees in daily life. Gay men were held in UMAP forced-labour camps from 1965 to 1968, working around 60 hours a week cutting cane and subjected to electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments; conscripts were paid seven pesos a day. Consensual same-sex acts left the Penal Code in 1979, and Fidel Castro publicly accepted blame for the UMAP record in 2010.

State institutions have campaigned for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s, and analysts of Cuban law record a persistent gap between the progressive formal framework and conditions of daily life.
localsOnly:
Residents face a labour statute that bars discrimination on sexual orientation but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground. Article 2(b) of the Labor Code (Law 116) covers orientation, so the constitutional promise of gender-identity protection has no matching employment clause; the trans-specific amendment debated in 2013 was not confirmed as enacted.

CENESEX has run a state-backed programme since the late 2000s covering a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education, giving residents an official channel that does not exist for citizens of most states.

Cuban authorities have used 'treason' and 'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who leave to seek asylum. Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to eight years in prison if they returned after filing asylum claims in the Netherlands in January 2018; a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018. LGBTI activists, including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation, remained under monitoring.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory carries no material on entry and visa rules, on whether border or immigration officers inspect passports or identity documents for gender markers, or on whether any screening process risks disclosure of a visitor's trans status. Those questions are unresolved here rather than answered.

Nothing sourced addresses access to gendered facilities, hate-crime legislation or its enforcement, or judicial decisions applying Article 42. Whether gender identity functions as a separate protected ground in employment enforcement is likewise unresolved: the Labor Code article names orientation only, and the final status of the trans-specific amendment proposed in 2013 is not confirmed in the sources.

The sources do not cover recognition of a foreign marriage or partner, or the treatment of foreign-issued documents, for a trans visitor. The reach of the July 2025 civil-registry reform beyond name changes is not specified.
